content.text: What if you could turn a magnet on and off? Electromagnets do exactly that—they create magnetic fields using electric current. From doorbells to MRI scanners, from electric motors to scrapyard cranes, electromagnets are essential to modern technology.

A current-carrying wire creates a magnetic field around it. Winding the wire into a solenoid concentrates this field, producing a pattern identical to a bar magnet. Adding a soft iron core creates an electromagnet.
When electric current flows through a wire, it creates a magnetic field around the wire.
Field is circular around the wire
Field exists only when current flows

content.text: To find the poles of a solenoid, use the right-hand grip rule: curl the fingers of your right hand in the direction of current flow around the coil, and your thumb points to the north pole. This is a frequently tested skill.
A wire carries current upward through a horizontal sheet of paper. Describe the magnetic field at the paper's surface.
Fingers curl anticlockwise when viewed from above
Field circles the wire anticlockwise (as seen from above)
Describe three ways to make an electromagnet stronger.
Increase the current through the coil
Increase the number of turns in the coil
Add a soft iron core inside the coil
An electromagnet is made using a steel core instead of soft iron. What problem might this cause?
Steel retains its magnetism after the current is switched off. The electromagnet would remain magnetic even when 'off', defeating the purpose of having a controllable magnet.
Current on: picks up iron/steel scrap
Can't pick up non-magnetic metals (copper, aluminium)

Electromagnet turns off, spring returns armature

A scrapyard uses an electromagnetic crane. Describe the advantages and disadvantages compared to a permanent magnet.
Can release the load by switching off
Can be much stronger than permanent magnets of the same size
Will drop load if power fails (safety issue)
Uses electricity continuously when holding load
— They create magnetism from electric current. No permanent magnet required.
— More TURNS increases strength, but just longer wire with same turns adds resistance without helping.
— Only ferromagnetic materials (iron, etc.) work as cores. Copper or aluminium won't help.
— The strongest magnets in the world are superconducting electromagnets.
— Reversing current reverses the polarity (swaps north and south poles).
To find how the number of turns affects electromagnet strength.
Wind wire around iron nail (10 turns)
Connect to power supply via ammeter
Set current to fixed value (e.g., 1 A)
Count how many paper clips the electromagnet can pick up
Plot graph of turns vs paper clips
More turns = more paper clips (stronger electromagnet).
Control: current, type of nail, size of paper clips
The three ways to increase the strength of an electromagnet are: increase the current, increase the number of turns of wire, and add a soft iron core. You can also bring the turns closer together.

Current flowing in a wire creates a circular magnetic field around it
Right-hand grip rule: thumb = current direction, fingers = field direction
Solenoid: coil of wire, acts like bar magnet when current flows
Stronger with: more current, more turns, iron core
Soft iron: easily magnetised and demagnetised
Applications: cranes, bells, relays, circuit breakers, MRI scanners
Advantage: can be switched on/off and strength controlled
— The field only exists while current flows; no current means no field. (recall)
Using the right-hand grip rule: thumb points downward (current direction), fingers curl clockwise when viewed from above.
— The field forms concentric circles whose direction is given by the curled fingers. (application)
Increase the current, increase the number of turns, add a soft iron core.
— Each factor concentrates or strengthens the magnetic flux. (recall)
Soft iron is easily magnetised and demagnetised. Steel retains magnetism, so the electromagnet would stay magnetic after the current is switched off, defeating the purpose of a controllable magnet.
— Soft iron allows rapid on/off switching. (explanation)

AC flows through the electromagnet, attracting the iron armature. The armature moves the hammer to strike the bell. Moving the armature breaks the circuit contact, the electromagnet turns off, and a spring returns the armature. This remakes the contact, restarting the cycle, producing a continuous ring.
The left end is the north pole.
— Looking from the right, current flows clockwise, which corresponds to a south pole at that end (S for clockwise). Therefore the opposite (left) end is north. (application)
Electromagnets can be switched off to release the load. Permanent magnets cannot drop scrap metal on demand. The strength of an electromagnet can also be adjusted.
